articles.content_excerpt: Let’s ETOC: HJC on the Class podcast! HJC Steering Committee members, Sebastian of Triangle DSA and Triangle Tenants Union, and Kelly of Boston DSA join the crew of the National Political Education Committee’s own Class podcast. They discuss the Emergency Tenant Organizing Committee (ETOC) and the exciting rise of tenant unionization on the socialist left. articles.title: Congress Must Investigate War Profiteers Once Again
articles.author: Hank Kennedy
articles.content_excerpt: In April, President Donald Trump requested a $445 billion increase to the defense budget, meaning the United States will be spending around $1.5 trillion on the military. Much of the largesse will benefit the Big Five war contractors: Boeing, General Dynamics, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, and RTX (formerly Raytheon). These are the companies behind such budget-shredding boondoggles as the F-35 and the littoral combat ships . If the promises of these weapons salesmen are to be believed, the US war with Iran should already be over. The enormousness of the Pentagon’s budget, on paper, means that any conflict the United States enters should be a decidedly short and lopsided affair. articles.title: Bernie Sanders’s 2016 Campaign Lit a Spark Beyond Elections
articles.author: Eric Blanc
articles.content_excerpt: Bernie Sanders’s impact on the American left is not typically measured in social movement terms. The story normally goes that democratic socialism returned to national politics after 2015, tens of thousands of people joined the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a new generation of socialist candidates ran for office, and a much larger left media ecosystem emerged. That’s all true. But another part of the story has received relatively less attention: the role Bernie’s campaigns played in inspiring and cohering a new generation of labor activists. I first started making this argument while writing about the red-state teachers’ revolt of 2018. articles.title: US Meddling in Brazil May Decide Latin America’s Future
articles.author: Benjamin Fogel
articles.content_excerpt: As Brazil heads toward Sunday’s presidential election first round, the contest is on a knife-edge. Polls show left-wing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva neck and neck with the ultraconservative Flávio Bolsonaro, the oldest of his imprisoned father’s brood. Jair Bolsonaro was defeated in 2022, as was the subsequent attempted coup that led to his criminal conviction. (He is now under house arrest.) Still, Bolsonarismo remained a powerful force. Compared to the high drama of four years ago, this campaign has at times seemed subdued, in part because most other candidates essentially offer duller, more gray-haired versions of Bolsonarismo. articles.title: The Battle of Cable Street Was an Antifascist Landmark
articles.author: David Rosenberg
articles.content_excerpt: Twenty years ago, I shared a platform with Aubrey Morris, one of the “ordinary” heroes of the Battle of Cable Street on October 4, 1936 — the iconic event in Britain’s prewar antifascist history. Aubrey was sixteen at the time, a Labour League of Youth member, and he still glowed with pride at having been part of the mass defiance that put the slogan “They shall not pass” into spectacular effect. He helped build barricades in Cable Street. Aubrey denied being a hero: “I did what any young Jewish boy would have done at that time.” Though he did have an additional motive. articles.title: The Stakes Are High in Brazil’s Upcoming Election
articles.author: Alex MacArthur
articles.content_excerpt: For a time this summer, Brazil’s presidential election seemed Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s to lose, and Latin America’s largest democracy appeared poised to hold its ground while right-wing candidates triumphed in Colombia, Peru, Honduras, Chile, and Panama, and the Left lost its long hold on Bolivia. Before, the race had been steadily tightening between the eighty-year-old president and his forty-five-year-old challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, the blandly affable, lacquered version of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a twenty-seven-year sentence for plotting a coup after his defeat. articles.title: West Point’s Honor Code Taught the Military to Lie
articles.author: Jasper Craven
articles.content_excerpt: On May 12, 1962, General Douglas MacArthur strode into the West Point mess hall and delivered a stirring farewell address before an audience of more than two thousand cadets. It had been just over a year since another famed former general, President Dwight D. Eisenhower, had famously delivered his own closing warning about industry’s capture of the Pentagon. Now MacArthur seemed worried about the corruption of the American soldier’s soul — the death of honor itself. Honor was everything to MacArthur.
